extracted.intended_audience: Readers of The Spectator; general literate public and aspiring writers interested in rhetoric, moral essays, and social conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing moral and rhetorical essays, character sketches, and tasteful amorous description in the style of early-18th-century periodical writing. Covers methods for evoking pity, modesty in erotic depiction, detecting hypocrisy, and the merits/origins of particular kinds of wit (e.g., punning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and origin of punning
rubrics_metrics.description: Punning is a 'mongrel miscreated' kind of wit—vulgar in many cases—but also an 'ancient innocent Diversion' that prevails in certain social circles; its prevalence may be owing to jovial convivial habits ("brown Juggs, muddy Belch," the 'Staincoat Hole') and the company in which it is practiced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains both the anti-pattern (punning as low, dazzling, benighting the faculties and producing 'melancholy Tincture') and a partial defence: that such diversion can distract from misguided innovations in wit. Gives social causes and humorous historical/examples (references to Mr. W--n and Mr. L--y). Use this to judge when puns are mere vulgarity versus an innocuous social pastime; beware of overvaluing or universalizing its merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work yourself up to genuine sorrow to evoke pity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Those who have laid down Rules for Rhetorick or Poetry, advise the Writer to work himself up, if possible, to the Pitch of Sorrow which he endeavours to produce in others." Grief has a natural eloquence and produces more moving sentiments than the finest imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: if the aim is to move readers to pity, the writer should cultivate genuine feeling (or convincingly simulate it) rather than rely solely on artifice. Anti-pattern: laboured, artificial pathos that lacks the immediacy of genuine sorrow. Example provided: Queen Ann Boleyn's letter as an instance of affecting, authentic expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer truth/fact and concise historical speeches to laboured fiction for pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: "The short Speeches, or Sentences which we often meet with in Histories, make a deeper Impression on the Mind of the Reader, than the most laboured Strokes in a well-written Tragedy." Truth and matter of fact set the person actually before us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for emotional impact, favor concise, factual statements or authentic documents over elaborate fictional description. Use short historical or epistolary excerpts to create immediacy (Ann Boleyn's letter is cited). Anti-pattern: overly rhetorical, embellished tragedy that distances the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity cannot be fully supplied by art
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nature on this Occasion dictates a thousand passionate things which cannot be supplied by Art." Those who indite their own sufferings stir up pity more than contrived invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage drawing on real feeling and genuine circumstance; synthetic or purely imagined passion tends to be less convincing. Use first-person or authentic documents where possible. This is both a stylistic and ethical criterion for persuasive moral writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty and the 'prevailing gentle Art' in amorous depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Modesty (a 'prevailing gentle Art' made of complaisance, courtship, and artful conformity) preserves desire and is more effective than forward obtrusion; a delicate, restrained presentation of a woman arouses imagination without becoming 'luscious' or loose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer indirectness, suggestion, and tender admiration to crude or explicit description. Positive examples: Antony's description of Cleopatra, Philip's pastorals, Ambrose Philips' stanzas. Anti-patterns: rusticity, broad expression, forward obtrusion, and 'licentious Language' which are said to offend and 'disgrace Humanity.' Use soft, restrained imagery and small gestures (an 'Ah' or 'Oh', a look, a sigh) to convey tenderness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid licentious/brutal language in erotic writing
rubrics_metrics.description: "Licentious Language has something brutal in it, which disgraces Humanity, and leaves us in the Condition of the Savages in the Field."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral and aesthetic rule: erotic or amorous passages should not be explicit or coarse. They should correct desire through tenderness and admiration rather than inciting or degrading it. Writers should alarm 'chaste Ears' against artful admirers who misuse gentle arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warn readers about platonic friendships that become amour
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship between persons of different sexes often conceals or leads into love; 'he is dangerous to be entertaind as a Friend or Visitant who is capable of gaining any eminent Esteem or Observation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As social-moral guidance and as a narrative device: portray cross-sex friendships cautiously, showing how approbation and kindness may escalate into passion. Anti-pattern: treating such friendships as indefinitely innocent; be alert to subtle escalation in behavior and feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for self-examination to detect hypocrisy
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover secret faults and self-deceit, examine yourself by (a) the rules of sacred writ and (b) the life of the exemplar who 'acted up to the Perfection of Human Nature.' Also: consider how you are characterized by enemies and friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive checklist-like guidance for moral self-assessment: compare yourself to religious/moral rules and exemplary figures; weigh praise and blame from others (friends may flatter; enemies may reveal faults). Use these retrospective comparisons to expose self-deceit and correct hidden vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to enemies' reproaches and question popular praise
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our Friends very often flatter us... An Adversary ... makes a stricter Search into us, discovers every Flaw..." Conversely, 'we should consider... how far we may deserve the Praises and Approbations which the World bestow upon us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical criterion for truthful self- or character-assessment: give due weight to critics and sceptics as they may reveal real defects; scrutinize popular praise to ensure it springs from worthy motives rather than vanity or faction. Use both perspectives to adjust self-judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspect doubtful virtues and beware partisan/intemperate zeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not lay too great a stress on virtues 'which are of a doubtful Nature'—particularly those where multitudes dissent. 'Intemperate Zeal, Bigotry and Persecution for any Party or Opinion... produce infinite Calamities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative rule for moral judgment and representation: avoid treating contested or partisan behaviors as unquestioned virtues. In writing and moral counsel, flag extremes of party zeal or bigotry as vices masked as virtues. Encourage circumspection where unanimity does not exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of bias introduced by natural constitution, passions, education, or interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions proceeding from 'natural Constitution, favourite Passions, particular Education, or whatever promotes our worldly Interest or Advantage' are inlets of prejudice and may pervert judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing characters (in oneself or others) or motives in narrative, explicitly interrogate whether inclinations arise from non-rational sources (habit, temperament, self-interest). Treat such motives as suspect and disclose them to avoid self-deceit or unreliable narration.
